subject: Anyone have tips for regression models for concentration data with many values below the detection limit?

messages.author: 0d1597ed161c7be7
messages.subject: Anyone have tips for regression models for concentration data with many values below the detection limit?
parts:
Hola!

I'm trying to estimate arsenic concentrations in drinking water wells that we couldn’t measure for a health study in Western Nevada.

The geostats expert on my committee suggested universal kriging with external drift. He said first I should develop a regression model and then probably do a spatial interpolation on the residuals.

Most arsenic values are near zero. The distribution has a long tail to the right, and is still not normal after a log transform. There are two peaks in the histogram, probably because hundreds of arsenic measurements were below the detection limit, so I assigned them a value near zero. Some of the arsenic kriging publications used normal score transforms.

My friend initially suggested a gamma poisson (negative binomial) model, but with many arsenic values below the detection limit, Noam suggested censored or truncated regression.

Mahalo nui loa!

messages.author: 2b27719db7267c87
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Re: Anyone have tips for regression models for concentration data with many values below the detection limit?
parts:
I don’t know anything about kriging, but when you mentioned that your distribution is still not normal after log transformation, I wondered whether the logit transformation would work better. Logit is the log odds of the proportion. I’ve been using it on percent data, so I divide by 100 first. If you have units such as parts per million, I think you would divide by a million first, etc. So, the transformation would look like this:

logit <- function(x) {log(x/(1-x))}
logit(some.ppm.data/1000000)

Bonnie

parts:
Found a package to deal with data below detection limits:
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/NADA/index.html

Non-detects are an old and common problem, as I expected, but maybe I show my age, at 37, when I forget to just type my question into google, as yu suggested!

According to Helsel 2005, "the worst practice when dealing with nondetects is to exclude or delete them. This produces a strong upward bias...Substituting values for nondetects" (like half the detection limit) should likewise be "considered unacceptable...There are better ways."

messages.subject: Re: Anyone have tips for regression models for concentration data with many values below the detection limit?
parts:
Dave,
I was advised to use NADA for concentration data with numerous NDs by a statistician from the UCD statistical laboratory.  I couldn't get MLE function (seemed like the best choice) to work with zeros and the stats man wrote me code for using cenfit function, but it didn't do what was intended; rather than infer the values below detection limit, it used the lowest value above MDL for every ND.  Helsel says you need at least 20% detections for it to function so might not work if you have mostly zeros.  I would like to figure out how to make NADA work but in the interest of not spending the rest of my life on it, I used simple substitution.

Bruno

Thanks Bruno!

I got cenreg to work but I see there's also cenmle, not sure what the difference is. I changed my zeroes to 0.001 so the automatic log transform wouldn't come back undefined. Could that be why it didn't work for you?

I only have about 20% ND (non-detects), sounds like you had a lot more. Helsel says that above about 50% ND's, "inferences about concentrations themselves must be abandoned and logistic regression employed." I guess logistic just means 0 vs.1, high vs. low, ND vs. detects.

parts:
Dave,
I tried changing my NDs that were zero to 0.00000001 and cenmle worked fine but as you know, that's not the reported value and I had committee members who were against it.  He was probably right, publishing augmented reported values may not fly, but I guess that is all simple substitution is anyway.  Looking at the sample datasets in NADA, Helsel doesn't include any with zero values, all reported values that are non-detects are greater than zero.  Its hard to imagine he didn't consider zeros being reported.

I can't quite remember if I had any detection frequencies below 20%.  As I understand >50% NDs, rank then plot all values, infer what the NDs would be based on the linear regression model.  One can use this method with any frequency of NDs.

If you haven't found Helsel 2005 "Non-detects and data analysis", check it out.  It's pretty comprehensive but I've only read portions and am far from an expert on the subject.

After this discussion I'm motivated to come to the D-RUG meetings.
Bruno

On Thursday, August 14, 2014 11:35:22 AM UTC-7, Dave Dauphine wrote:
Thanks Bruno!

I got cenreg to work but I see there's also cenmle, not sure what the difference is. I changed my zeroes to 0.001 so the automatic log transform wouldn't come back undefined. Could that be why it didn't work for you?

I only have about 20% ND (non-detects), sounds like you had a lot more. Helsel says that above about 50% ND's, "inferences about concentrations themselves must be abandoned and logistic regression employed." I guess logistic just means 0 vs.1, high vs. low, ND vs. detects. 


2014-08-14 10:11 GMT-07:00 bruno pitton <bruno...@gmail.com>:
Dave,
I was advised to use NADA for concentration data with numerous NDs by a statistician from the UCD statistical laboratory.  I couldn't get MLE function (seemed like the best choice) to work with zeros and the stats man wrote me code for using cenfit function, but it didn't do what was intended; rather than infer the values below detection limit, it used the lowest value above MDL for every ND.  Helsel says you need at least 20% detections for it to function so might not work if you have mostly zeros.  I would like to figure out how to make NADA work but in the interest of not spending the rest of my life on it, I used simple substitution.

Bruno


On Thursday, August 7, 2014 7:11:50 PM UTC-7, Dave Dauphine wrote:

Hola!

I'm trying to estimate arsenic concentrations in drinking water wells that we couldn’t measure for a health study in Western Nevada.

The geostats expert on my committee suggested universal kriging with external drift. He said first I should develop a regression model and then probably do a spatial interpolation on the residuals.

Most arsenic values are near zero. The distribution has a long tail to the right, and is still not normal after a log transform. There are two peaks in the histogram, probably because hundreds of arsenic measurements were below the detection limit, so I assigned them a value near zero. Some of the arsenic kriging publications used normal score transforms.

My friend initially suggested a gamma poisson (negative binomial) model, but with many arsenic values below the detection limit, Noam suggested censored or truncated regression.

Mahalo nui loa!

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Re: Anyone have tips for regression models for concentration data with many values below the detection limit?
parts:
"Seems like anything under the detection limit would be same right?"  By this you mean, all data below detection limit would be given the same value?  Yes and no.  They are given slightly different values based on their ranking, but you could figure out the mean of those values based on the mean of the whole dataset and the known data.  But one should only use these methods for summary stats, not use their assigned values.

I'm a novice in stats and R too.  But it would good to change that.

messages.author: 0d1597ed161c7be7
messages.subject: How to choose the best model with censored outcome data
parts:
Hi again!

From the error message below I'm guessing the "step" function does not work with an mle, which is an S4 class?

I can get the step function to choose the best model by AIC for an lm, and it says it should also work for glm's, but so far I've only seen mle's in the Non Detects and Data Analysis (NADA) package I'm using because ~20% of my outcome data was below the detection limit. 

The "step" code is far simpler than what my friend showed me for comparing AIC's from Statistical Rethinking, but I guess I'll see if the latter will work with the NADA package. 

The NADA package provides a x2 test to compare models, but for some reason all my models have huge x2's with p=0, so I don't know how to compare this way either (example below).

Thanks again DRUGgies!


install.packages("NADA")
library(NADA)
As_nada_mle=with(clean2503, cenreg(Cen(As001, nd_epa)~Elev_m + Tahoe + Walker + UpperCarson + Tcan2car + TruckeeTribOrMain))
Best_nada=step(As_nada_mle)
